Hold it up to the light: agate lets a little light through at thin edges (Michigan EGLE 2024). Look for bands or moss: \"the bands so commonly seen in agates are edges of layers deposited in irregular cavities\" (Dole 1950 p.17). A shell-shaped break does not tell it from quartzite: conchoidal fracture \"is typical of quartz\" (Dole 1950), and both are quartz.","not_it":"Quartzite, the commonest pebble in old Columbia gravels (RI16 p.21: \"quartzite is particularly abundant\"), is quartz sand cemented so tightly the grains barely show, with a glassy shine on fresh surfaces (Dole 1950 p.36), and no bands. Jasper is opaque (Dake 1938). Chert weathers to a white or light grey skin (RI16). Basalt is dark and dull (our reading, not a source's). In basalt country the basalt itself is \"mostly barren\" and its fillings \"too small\" (RI16 pp.13, 15): look in the gravels, not the basalt faces."}
